title: 4Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every quadruplet with a dedup set versus sorting and nested two pointers.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an array nums and an integer target, return every unique quadruplet of four numbers from the array that sum exactly to target.

blocks.caption: Sort the array, fix two values with nested loops, then two pointers find the remaining pair

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given an array nums and an integer target, return every unique quadruplet of four numbers from the array that sum exactly to target.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Every Way Four Coins Add Up to an Exact Total
blocks.text: Like searching a pile of coins of different denominations for every distinct combination of exactly four coins that adds up to one specific total amount, without listing the same combination twice.

blocks.caption: Find every distinct combination of four numbers that sums to the target

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2], target = 0

blocks.content: {"headers":["Quadruplet","Sum","Why"],"rows":[["[-2, -1, 1, 2]","-2 + -1 + 1 + 2 = 0","These four distinct values, taken from the array, sum exactly to the target"],["[-2, 0, 0, 2]","-2 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 0","Both copies of 0 present in nums are used here, alongside -2 and 2"],["[-1, 0, 0, 1]","-1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 0","The other valid combination using both copies of 0, alongside -1 and 1"]]}

blocks.text: Example: nums = [2, 2, 2, 2, 2], target = 8

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The only possible combination of four values is 2, 2, 2, 2","summing to 8","With every value identical, there is exactly one possible multiset of four values to choose, regardless of which specific indices are picked"],["Answer","[[2, 2, 2, 2]]","Only one distinct quadruplet exists, even though many different index combinations produce it"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: fewer than 4 elements in nums
If nums has fewer than four elements, no quadruplet can even be formed, so the answer is an empty list.
5. How Should We Think?

Before searching for four values independently, notice this is structurally identical to 3Sum, just with one extra value to fix first, and 3Sum itself was already "fix one value, then two-pointer scan for the remaining pair".

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Finding 4 values summing to a target can be broken down as "fix the first value, then find 3 remaining values summing to target minus that first value", which is exactly the 3Sum sub-problem.

Observation 2: 3Sum itself breaks down the same way: "fix one value, then find 2 remaining values summing to a reduced target", which is the two-pointer Two Sum II structure.

Observation 3: So 4Sum is really just two nested "fix one value" layers wrapped around the same sorted two-pointer core: fix the first value, fix the second value, searching only from where the first left off, then two pointers scan the rest for the final pair.

Observation 4: Sorting up front is what makes both the two-pointer scan and duplicate avoidance direct: once sorted, any repeated value sits immediately next to its duplicates, so skipping "the same value as last time" at any of the four positions is a simple adjacent-element check, no set or hash map needed at all.

Whenever a k-Sum problem needs one more fixed value than a version already solved, wrap one more nested loop, with duplicate-skipping, around the existing solution's core, rather than re-deriving the whole approach from scratch.
This same nesting keeps working for 5Sum, 6Sum, or general k-Sum: each additional fixed value costs one more loop, but the innermost two-pointer scan for the final pair never changes.
6. Brute Force Solution
Check every combination of four indices directly, summing their values and collecting every distinct combination that matches the target, using a set of sorted tuples to avoid duplicates.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every combination of four indices, check whether the four values sum to target.
If they do, sort the four values and add them to a set of found quadruplets, so duplicates collapse automatically.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The four nested loops enforce a strict increasing order among the four indices, so the same 4 indices are never checked in more than one order, and no index is ever reused within a single quadruplet.

Sorting the 4 values before storing them normalizes each found quadruplet into one canonical form, since the same 4 values could otherwise be discovered via different index orders and look like different results.
A set, not a list, collects the found quadruplets specifically because duplicate values, not just duplicate index combinations, need to collapse into a single entry in the final answer.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible quadruplet of indices is checked, and the set removes duplicates, so this is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n to the 4th power), for the four nested loops.
Space: O(n), for the set of found quadruplets, not counting the output.

Limitation: exactly like 3Sum, sorting the array first and using two pointers for the last two positions turns two of the four nested loops into a linear scan, and makes duplicate skipping direct instead of relying on a set.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Checking all n to the 4th power index combinations and deduplicating afterward does two things the sorted structure could instead prevent from ever happening: it repeats work across index orders that are guaranteed to produce the same value combination, and it relies on a set, extra memory, hashing overhead, to clean up duplicates that never needed to be generated in the first place. Sorting first means every duplicate value sits adjacent to its copies, so skipping "try this exact value again at this position" is a single comparison against the previous position, not a lookup. And exactly as in 3Sum, once two values are fixed, the remaining two-value sub-problem is answered by the same converging two-pointer scan, since it is now just a smaller Two-Sum-on-sorted-array problem, needing no further nested search.

Sort the array first. Fix the first two values using two nested loops, skipping duplicate values at each position, then use two pointers on the remaining subarray to find pairs summing to the required remaining target, exactly like the two pointer step in 3Sum, just one level deeper.
9. Optimized Solution
Sort the array, fix the first two values with nested loops, then two pointers for the last two.
Dry run for sorted nums = [-2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2], target = 0

blocks.content: {"headers":["First value","Second value","Remaining target","Two-pointer outcome","Why"],"rows":[["-2","-1","3","left starts at 0, right at 2; after left advances past two 0s, 1 + 2 = 3 matches, found [-2,-1,1,2]","0 and then another 0 are each tried against 2 but fall short of 3, until left reaches 1, whose sum with 2 exactly hits the remaining target"],["-2","0 (first occurrence)","2","left at 0, right at 2: 0 + 2 = 2 matches immediately, found [-2,0,0,2]","The very first pointer positions already sum to exactly the remaining target, so no pointer movement is needed before recording this quadruplet"],["-1","0","1","left at 0, right at 2: 0 + 2 = 2 exceeds 1, right moves inward; then 0 + 1 = 1 matches, found [-1,0,0,1]","The initial pair overshoots the remaining target, so the right pointer steps inward to a smaller value until the sum exactly matches"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: sort first, fix the first two values, two pointers for the remaining pair

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), two nested loops for the first two values times a linear two pointer scan for the last two.
Space: O(log n) to O(n) depending on the sort, not counting the output.
Why This Works

Fixing the first two values and sorting the remainder reduces the problem to exactly Two Sum II on the sub-array after them: find two values summing to a known remaining target, which the standard converging two-pointer scan solves directly. Skipping past any value equal to the one just tried, at all four positions, first value, second value, left pointer, right pointer, guarantees that no combination of values, not just indices, is ever recorded more than once, since two different index choices that would produce identical quadruplet values are always adjacent to each other once sorted.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Duplicate-skip location","What it prevents"],"rows":[["Skipping a repeated first value","Re-running the entire inner search with an identical starting value, which would rediscover the exact same quadruplets"],["Skipping a repeated second value","Re-running the two-pointer scan with an identical pair of fixed values, again finding the same quadruplets"],["Skipping repeated left/right pointer values after a match","Recording the same value combination again immediately after finding it, before the pointers have moved past all copies of it"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The outer two loops run i up to n minus 3 and j up to n minus 2, not all the way to the end, since at least 2 more values, for left and right, must remain available after i and j.

The duplicate checks are guarded by requiring i (or j) to not be the very first candidate at that level, so the first occurrence of a value at each level is never mistakenly skipped, only repeats of a value already tried are.
remaining is computed as target minus both fixed values, reducing the inner search to a plain Two-Sum-style target for the two-pointer scan.

After recording a match, both left and right are advanced past any remaining duplicates of their own just-used value, before the next comparison, preventing the same quadruplet from being recorded a second time.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

4Sum is exactly 3Sum with one more layer of fixed values wrapped around the same sort-plus-two-pointer core, and this same pattern extends naturally to 5Sum, 6Sum, and general k-Sum problems, each adding one more nested loop around the same two pointer base case.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to skip duplicates at all four levels, first value, second value, left pointer, right pointer, any one of which alone can still let duplicate quadruplets through even if the other three are handled correctly.
Integer overflow when summing four values or computing the remaining target, which is why intermediate sums should be computed using a wider integer type than a standard 32-bit int.

Only checking whether a position is not the very first candidate, without also confirming the current value actually equals the previous one, which would skip valid, non-duplicate positions by mistake.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Fewer than 4 elements in nums","Cannot form any quadruplet at all, and the outer loop bounds correctly prevent it from ever executing"],["An array of all identical values","Produces at most one distinct quadruplet regardless of how many times that value repeats, since the duplicate-skipping logic collapses every repeated attempt"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Present this explicitly as "3Sum with an extra fixed value", since recognizing that the same sort-plus-two-pointer core generalizes directly is more valuable than treating this as an unrelated new problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find all unique quadruplets or k-tuples summing to a target" points toward "k minus 2 nested loops fixing values, then a two-pointer scan for the final pair", reusing the exact same sort-plus-two-pointer core regardless of k.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you generalize this to a general k-Sum function? Write a recursive helper that fixes one value and reduces to (k minus 1)-Sum, with the base case being exactly this two-pointer pair-finding step at k equals 2.

What if the array could contain very large values, close to the integer overflow boundary? Use a wider integer type for every intermediate sum and the remaining target calculation, exactly as done here, to avoid silent overflow errors.

How would you count the number of quadruplets instead of listing them, when nums could be very large? Counting exactly is harder combinatorially with duplicates present; a common approach uses a hash map of pairwise sums, similar to 4Sum II, if only a count, not the actual index positions, is needed and the array is not required to stay sorted.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Directly extends 3Sum by one more fixed-value layer, which itself directly extends Two Sum II's two-pointer core by one fixed-value layer.
Same sort-then-skip-adjacent-duplicates technique used in 3Sum, applied here at two levels of fixed values instead of one.
Same underlying idea as general k-Sum, where k minus 2 values are fixed by nested loops before falling back to the same two-pointer base case.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n to the 4th power) time, O(n) space for deduplication.
Optimized: O(n cubed) time, O(log n) to O(n) space from sorting.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Sort, fix two values with nested duplicate-skipping loops, then two pointers for the remaining pair
Core Idea: 4Sum reduces to 3Sum reduces to Two Sum II, each layer fixing one more value before falling back to the same converging two-pointer scan
Time: O(n cubed)
Space: O(log n) to O(n), from the sort itself
Most Important Observation: A k-Sum problem is k minus 2 nested "fix one value, skip duplicates" loops wrapped around the same sorted two-pointer pair-finding core
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: 4Sum is 3Sum is Two Sum II, just with more values fixed first
